subtopic: Theorem of remote interior angles of a triangle
stem: The measures of angles of a triangle are in the ratio \(5 : 6 : 7\). Find the measures.
solution:
Let the measures of the angles of a triangle be \(5x\), \(6x\), \(7x\).
\(\therefore 5x + 6x + 7x = 180^\circ\)
\(18x = 180^\circ\)
\(x = 10^\circ\)
\(5x = 5 \times 10 = 50^\circ\), \(6x = 6 \times 10 = 60^\circ\), \(7x = 7 \times 10 = 70^\circ\)
\(\therefore\) the measures of angles of the triangle are \(50^\circ\), \(60^\circ\) and \(70^\circ\).

subtopic: Theorem of remote interior angles of a triangle
stem:
Observe figure 3.4 and find the measures of \(\angle PRS\) and \(\angle RTS\).

In figure 3.4, the points Q, R, S are collinear with R between Q and S; the point T lies on seg PR and seg TS is drawn. \(\angle PQR = 40^\circ\), \(\angle QPR = 30^\circ\) and \(\angle TSR = 20^\circ\).
solution:
\(\angle PRS\) is an exterior angle of \(\triangle PQR\).
So from the theorem of remote interior angles,
\(\angle PRS = \angle PQR + \angle QPR\)
\(= 40^\circ + 30^\circ\)
\(= 70^\circ\)
In \(\triangle RTS\)
\(\angle TRS + \angle RTS + \angle TSR = 180^\circ\) ........ sum of all angles of a triangle
T lies on seg PR, so ray RT is the same as ray RP and hence \(\angle TRS = \angle PRS = 70^\circ\); also \(\angle TSR = 20^\circ\).
\(\therefore 70^\circ + \angle RTS + 20^\circ = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle RTS + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle RTS = 90^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle PRS = 70^\circ\) and \(\angle RTS = 90^\circ\).
diagramNote: Fig. 3.4 — ray QS with R between Q and S; P above, joined to Q and to S; T on seg PR joined to S. Marked: \(\angle QPR = 30^\circ\) at P, \(\angle PQR = 40^\circ\) at Q, \(\angle TSR = 20^\circ\) at S.
_note: The book prints this worked solution with FOUR empty fill-in boxes, which are completed here: (1) the right-hand side of the angle-sum line \(= 180^\circ\); (2) \(\angle TRS = 70^\circ\); (3) \(\angle TSR = 20^\circ\); (4) \(\angle RTS = 90^\circ\). Boxes (2) and (3) are confirmed by the book's own very next printed line, \(\angle RTS + 90^\circ = 180^\circ\), since \(70 + 20 = 90\). The sentence identifying \(\angle TRS\) with \(\angle PRS\) is added here because the book leaves that step implicit.

subtopic: Theorem of remote interior angles of a triangle
stem: Prove that the sum of exterior angles of a triangle, obtained by extending its sides in the same direction is \(360^\circ\).
solution:
Given : \(\angle PAB\), \(\angle QBC\) and \(\angle ACR\) are exterior angles of \(\triangle ABC\).
(In fig. 3.5 the sides of \(\triangle ABC\) are extended in the same direction — ray CA beyond A to P, ray AB beyond B to Q, and ray BC beyond C to R.)

To prove : \(\angle PAB + \angle QBC + \angle ACR = 360^\circ\)

Proof :

Method I
Considering exterior \(\angle PAB\) of \(\triangle ABC\), \(\angle ABC\) and \(\angle ACB\) are its remote interior angles.
\(\angle PAB = \angle ABC + \angle ACB\) ----(I)
Similarly, \(\angle ACR = \angle ABC + \angle BAC\) ----(II) ..theorem of remote interior angles
and \(\angle CBQ = \angle BAC + \angle ACB\) ---- (III)
Adding (I), (II) and (III),
\(\angle PAB + \angle ACR + \angle CBQ\)
\(= \angle ABC + \angle ACB + \angle ABC + \angle BAC + \angle BAC + \angle ACB\)
\(= 2\angle ABC + 2\angle ACB + 2\angle BAC\)
\(= 2 (\angle ABC + \angle ACB + \angle BAC)\)
\(= 2 \times 180^\circ\) ..... sum of interior angles of a triangle
\(= 360^\circ\)

Method II
In fig. 3.6 the interior angles of \(\triangle ABC\) are \(\angle a = \angle BAC\), \(\angle b = \angle ABC\), \(\angle c = \angle ACB\) and the exterior angles are \(\angle d = \angle PAB\), \(\angle e = \angle QBC\), \(\angle f = \angle ACR\).
\(\angle c + \angle f = 180^\circ\) .... (angles in linear pair)
Also, \(\angle a + \angle d = 180^\circ\)
and \(\angle b + \angle e = 180^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle c + \angle f + \angle a + \angle d + \angle b + \angle e = 180^\circ \times 3 = 540^\circ\)
\(\angle f + \angle d + \angle e + (\angle a + \angle b + \angle c) = 540^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle f + \angle d + \angle e + 180^\circ = 540^\circ\)
\(\therefore f + d + e = 540^\circ - 180^\circ\)
\(= 360^\circ\)
diagramNote: Two figures. Fig. 3.5 — \(\triangle ABC\) with each side extended in the same direction to P (beyond A), Q (beyond B) and R (beyond C). Fig. 3.6 — the same figure with the three interior angles labelled \(a\) (at A), \(b\) (at B), \(c\) (at C) and the three exterior angles labelled \(d\) (at A), \(e\) (at B), \(f\) (at C).
_note: The book prints two methods for this example; both are transcribed in the single solution, labelled Method I and Method II. The final two lines of Method II are printed by the book without the angle sign (as \(f + d + e\)) and are transcribed as printed. The sentence naming which angle each letter \(a\)-\(f\) stands for is added so Method II is readable without fig. 3.6.

subtopic: Theorem of remote interior angles of a triangle
stem:
In figure 3.7, bisectors of \(\angle B\) and \(\angle C\) of \(\triangle ABC\) intersect at point P. Prove that \(\angle BPC = 90 + \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC\).
Complete the proof filling in the blanks.
solution:
Proof : In \(\triangle ABC\),
\(\angle BAC + \angle ABC + \angle ACB = 180^\circ\) ...... sum of measures of angles of a triangle
\(\therefore \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC + \frac{1}{2} \angle ABC + \frac{1}{2} \angle ACB = \frac{1}{2} \times 180^\circ\) ....multiplying each term by \(\frac{1}{2}\)
Seg BP bisects \(\angle ABC\) and seg CP bisects \(\angle ACB\), so \(\frac{1}{2} \angle ABC = \angle PBC\) and \(\frac{1}{2} \angle ACB = \angle PCB\).
\(\therefore \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC + \angle PBC + \angle PCB = 90^\circ\)
\(\therefore \angle PBC + \angle PCB = 90^\circ - \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC\) ......(I)
In \(\triangle BPC\)
\(\angle BPC + \angle PBC + \angle PCB = 180^\circ\) ......sum of measures of angles of a triangle
\(\therefore \angle BPC + (90^\circ - \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC) = 180^\circ\) ......from (I)
\(\therefore \angle BPC = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC)\)
\(= 180^\circ - 90^\circ + \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC\)
\(= 90^\circ + \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC\)
diagramNote: Fig. 3.7 — \(\triangle ABC\) with A at the top and BC as the base. The bisector of \(\angle B\) and the bisector of \(\angle C\) are drawn as dashed segments meeting at P inside the triangle; the two halves at B carry matching arc marks and the two halves at C carry matching cross marks.
_note: The book prints this proof with THREE empty fill-in boxes, which are completed here: (1) the right-hand side of the angle-sum line \(= 180^\circ\); (2) the right-hand side after \(\frac{1}{2} \times\) is \(180^\circ\); (3) the box in \(\angle BPC + \Box = 180^\circ\) is \(90^\circ - \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC\), i.e. the left side of (I) — confirmed by the book's own next printed line \(\angle BPC = 180^\circ - (90^\circ - \frac{1}{2} \angle BAC)\). The sentence identifying \(\frac{1}{2} \angle ABC\) with \(\angle PBC\) (and likewise at C) is added because the book makes that substitution silently. Book quirk transcribed as printed: the statement writes '90' with no degree sign while the proof body uses \(90^\circ\).
